questions.prompt: After a request times out with no response, what do you actually know about the outcome?

options.text: It's unknown — the operation may have succeeded and the reply was lost, or it never arrived

questions.explanation: A timeout is ambiguous: the client can't tell whether the operation ran and the response was lost, or the request never arrived. This is why blind retries are dangerous.

questions.prompt: Why add jitter to exponential backoff?

options.text: So clients that failed together don't retry in lockstep and re-overload the service

questions.explanation: Jitter randomizes the wait so a crowd of clients spreads their retries over time instead of hitting the recovering service in a synchronized wave.

questions.prompt: How does an idempotency key make a non-idempotent write (like a charge) safe to retry?

options.text: The server records the key's result and returns it on a retry, instead of performing the operation again

questions.explanation: The same key is sent on every retry; the server recognizes it and returns the stored result, so the charge happens at most once.

options.text: Many clients retrying a failing dependency at once, amplifying load and cascading the failure

questions.explanation: Synchronized, unbounded retries pile load onto a service exactly when it's weakest, often finishing it off. Backoff, jitter, retry caps, and circuit breakers prevent it.

questions.prompt: What is the risk of setting a timeout too long?

options.text: Threads, connections, and memory stay tied up waiting on a dead peer, risking resource exhaustion

questions.explanation: An overly long timeout leaks resources on a dead dependency, which can cascade into a wider outage. Too short, and you get false failures. Tune deliberately.

questions.prompt: Which operations are naturally safe to retry without special handling? Select all that apply.

options.text: PUT (replace a resource with a full new value)

questions.explanation: GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent, so repeating them has the same effect as doing them once. POST is not idempotent and needs an idempotency key.
